newsitem.title: USA: Commerce error briefly dims brighter U.S. trade picture.
newsitem.headline: Commerce error briefly dims brighter U.S. trade picture.

text.p: A billion-dollar mistake by the Commerce Department in reporting the February trade deficit on Thursday temporarily obscured a significant decline in the monthly shortfall.

The Commerce Department announced late in the day that after correcting for "reporting errors" on oil imports, the February deficit actually dropped 17.9 percent from $12.67 billion in January to $10.4 billion. Earlier, it had announced the monthly gap narrowed only by 8.5 percent to $11.59 billion.

A booming U.S. economy still drew in hefty imports during February but not at quite as fast a clip as the government first thought. Several analysts said they could not recall seeing such a huge correction in the trade report on the day it was issued.

After spending hours checking its figures after news reports said there was a possible error, the Commerce Department said about $1.1 billion of oil imports that had entered the country earlier had incorrectly been reported as arriving in February and had to be subtracted from its monthly estimate.
While it altered the overall monthly deficit, analysts said the correction did not change the fact of big and persistent gaps in bilateral U.S. deficits with key Asian trade dynamos Japan and China.
They added it will be hard to shrink these two-way deficits while a soaring U.S. dollar makes popular Japanese cars and other imported goods cheaper for eager American consumers.
Economist Lawrence Chimerine of the Economic Strategy Institute in Washington said first-quarter economic growth may now be revised up since the import bill is not quite as high.
"Monthly numbers are erratic... but a billion dollars is not an insignificant amount," Chimerine said of the error.
Exports rose 4 percent in February to a record $73.46 billion, helped by a bulge in commercial aircraft sales to Britain and by a modest fall in costs for imported oil and other energy.
Economists said that a rising dollar and higher imports helped keep U.S. consumer prices in check but also set the stage for long-term problems.

"Right now, we need this to let some steam out of an overheating economy," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis. "But long term, it's quite worrisome because these deficits are actually rising on a trend basis."

Separately on Thursday, the Labour Department said new applications for jobless benefits picked up last week to 332,000 from 324,000 in the previous week -- possibly also a helpful development in the short run.
"The data suggest that the momentum in the labour force may be leveling out," said William Sullivan, senior vice-president of Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. in New York.

The Federal Reserve, which raised short-term interest rates a quarter percentage point late last month, has cited its concern that tight labour markets risk ingniting inflationary wage demands and price rises.
Fed Vice-Chairwoman Alice Rivlin, speaking to a business group Thursday, said she saw no sign the economy was "running out of steam or generating any obvious imbalances."
She said central bank policy-makers were exercising "prudence and a bit of insurance" when they raised rates to sustain the long-running expansion, now in its seventh year.

A report from the Federal Reserve bank of Philadelphia said its index of manufacturing activity dropped sharply to 5.7 in April from 21.1 in March as new orders waned and hiring weakened, while prices for goods accelerated.
Economist Michael Trebing of the Philadelphia Fed said there clearly was "some slowing in the growth rate" regionally but cautioned it might not mean a national slowdown.

The trade report showed a strong improvement in business with Western Europe, where the United States posted a surplus of $291 million in February -- a sharp reversal from January's $1.34 billion deficit.
Most of that was because exports of commercial aircraft quadrupled to more than $1 billion in February from $263 million in January.
The trade picture with Asia remained muddied.

The politically sensitive deficit with Japan -- the biggest with any single country -- was down 0.9 percent to $4.26 billion. The shortfall with China narrowed 9.6 percent from January to $3.37 billion but exports to China actually were lower in February.

"We're now facing a double-whammy. Every single month Japan and China are giving us a one-two punch and in the future it's going to be China that is leading the assault," said Sohn. He noted China was primarily buying high-tech machinery from the United States with the intent to further boost its manufactured exports.
Commerce Secretary William Daley said China was a worry.

"China remains the only major market in the world where U.S. exports are not growing," Daley told a news conference. "This export picture remains an object of concern to me and to the administration.'
